subsystems.name: Ribbon
subsystems.role: the load-bearing cable that extends from the equator to beyond geostationary orbit.
parts: carbon nanotube or boron nitride nanotube composite fibres
protective coating against atomic oxygen and ultraviolet light

subsystems.name: Anchor
subsystems.role: holds the lower end of the ribbon at Earth's surface near the equator.

subsystems.name: Counterweight
subsystems.role: provides tension by hanging beyond geostationary orbit, keeping the ribbon taut.

subsystems.name: Climbers
subsystems.role: robotic vehicles that carry payloads up and down the ribbon.

subsystems.name: Power beaming
subsystems.role: supplies energy to climbers without heavy onboard power sources.

subsystems.name: Debris and hazard management
subsystems.role: avoids collisions with orbital debris and damps dangerous oscillations.
parts: active damping thrusters along the ribbon

buildSteps.title: Synthesise long nanotubes
buildSteps.detail: Grow defect-free carbon or boron nitride nanotubes in lengths of kilometres — today only centimetres to tens of centimetres are possible in the lab.

buildSteps.title: Weave the ribbon
buildSteps.detail: Assemble nanotubes into a composite ribbon with the required specific strength and flexibility, using spinning and cross-linking techniques.

buildSteps.title: Deploy a seed ribbon from orbit
buildSteps.detail: Launch a small spool to geostationary orbit, then unreel it downward toward Earth and upward for the counterweight.

buildSteps.title: Anchor to Earth
buildSteps.detail: Attach the lower end to a floating platform at the equator and secure it against wind and currents.

buildSteps.title: Raise the counterweight
buildSteps.detail: Move a mass beyond geostationary orbit using solar-electric propulsion until the ribbon is under tension.

buildSteps.title: Build climbers and power beaming
buildSteps.detail: Develop robotic climbers and ground-based laser stations to power their ascent.

buildSteps.title: Test and operate
buildSteps.detail: Send payloads up the ribbon, monitor for damage from debris and radiation, and repair or replace sections as needed.

prerequisites.why: no material yet combines the required specific strength (tens of GPa·cm³/g) with the kilometre-scale defect-free lengths needed.
existing networks track only larger objects; millimetre-scale debris could sever the ribbon.
demonstrated at kilowatt scales, but megawatt-class continuous beams are needed to lift climbers.
we can assemble structures in orbit, but deploying and controlling a 35,000 km ribbon is far beyond current practice.
climbers must ascend 35,000 km carrying payloads without heavy power sources or motors.

pathway.milestone: produce metre-scale ribbons with tensile strength approaching theoretical limits
pathway.unlocks: proof that the required material can exist outside theory.

pathway.milestone: deploy a kilometre-scale ribbon and test climber traction and dynamics
pathway.unlocks: understanding of deployment, oscillation control and debris avoidance.

pathway.milestone: deploy a small ribbon to geostationary orbit and lift a small payload
pathway.unlocks: validation of the full-scale architecture and power beaming.

pathway.milestone: a ribbon from the equator to beyond geostationary orbit capable of routine payload transport
pathway.unlocks: low-cost access to space and planetary export.
